To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CypD ablates are associated with increased mt-HK activity in normoxic, glucose only-perfusions, and in glucose, glutamine-pyruvate-lactate-perfusion models.
in glucose-only perfused hearts, deletion CypD is neither associated with end-ischaemic mitochondrial hexokinase binding nor with increased protection against ischaemia/reperfusion injury.
CypD ablated hearts have increased mitochondrial hexokinase II activity in normoxic and ischemic hearts, which is associated with increased protection against I.R. injury.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether the absence of CypD affects the amount of mitochondrial hexokinase (mtHK), a key enzyme in the regulation of glycolysis.
the effect of CypD on mtHKII in normoxic and I/R mouse hearts.
the role of cyclophilins in the heart.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of CypD does not influence end-ischemic HKII binding in hearts perfused with glucose.
CypD is involved in mitochondrial HK binding, but that this is not the only determinant.
CypD abrogation increases the amount of mitochondrial bound hexo-kinase in hearts subjected to ischemia in presence of multiple substrates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CypD is a key regulator of mtHKII binding to mitochondria in the heart.
CypD ablates is not sufficient for increased mtHK binding, but is required for the full protection by IPC.
in glucose only-perfusion, CypD is dispensable for the end-ischemic increase in mtHKII activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CypD deletion is a more potent protection mechanism than mtHK binding.
the amount of mt-HK is determined by the metabolic state of the cell.

the presence of CypD in the mitochondria is not associated with the amount of mt-HK present in the mitochondria, and therefore the protective effect of CypD ablaton against I/R injury is independent of mt-HK.
